question: Sudden cessation of ear discharge (drying of the ear) in a patient with active squamosal CSOM who then develops headache and fever should be treated as a probable intracranial complication until proven otherwise.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Incorrect. This statement is true and represents a critical clinical trap. Sudden drying of the ear combined with new systemic symptoms in squamosal CSOM should raise immediate suspicion of an intracranial complication — the discharge may have been diverted intracranially rather than externally.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. This is a classic and dangerous trap: the ear appearing to 'dry up' can mean that the normal discharge pathway has been blocked — for example, by a large cholesteatoma or granulation tissue — while infection has spread intracranially. New headache and fever in this context mandate urgent CT/MRI and neurosurgical consultation.
